samples.summary: Markdown URL gate lets `<` / `>` through, enabling an angle-bracket link-destination bypass and raw-HTML injection into the exported `.md`
samples.evidence:
`isEmittableUrl()` (markdown.ts:295-300) refuses whitespace/C0-C1 controls and then routes on `HAS_SCHEME = /^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9+.-]*:/`. A destination that *starts with* `<` never matches `HAS_SCHEME`, so it is classified as a harmless relative reference and emitted verbatim (`escapeMarkdownHref`, line 396, escapes only `\` and `)` — never `<` or `>`, even though `escapeMarkdownText` at line 374 does escape `<` in body text precisely because it is dangerous).

Attacker path (identical provenance to the one the diff's own comments cite: HTML paste, DOCX/HTML import, a collaborator's CRDT write into `style.href` / `image.src`), then victim exports via the new Export → Markdown entry (`packages/frontend/src/app/docs/text-actions.ts:44`) or `wafflebase docs content --format md`:

1. `href = "<javascript:alert(1)>"` → gate passes → output `[t](<javascript:alert\(1\)>)`. CommonMark's first link-destination form is "a sequence of characters between an opening `<` and a closing `>`", with backslash escapes processed, so the rendered href is exactly `javascript:alert(1)` — the one value the whole gate exists to block.
2. `href = "<script>alert(1)</script>"` (no whitespace, so `UNEMITTABLE_URL_CHARS` does not fire) → output `[t](<script>alert\(1\)</script>)`. The link fails to parse (destination `<script>` is not followed by whitespace/`)`), the run degrades to literal text, and `<script>`/`</script>` are then re-parsed as CommonMark *inline raw HTML* — so the exported document renders `<script>alert(1)</script>` in any renderer that does not strip HTML.
3. The same `<…>` wrapper defeats the image gate: `src = "<data:text/html;base64,…>"` fails both `/^data:/i` (so the `inlineImages:false` placeholder branch is skipped, markdown.ts:330) and `SAFE_IMAGE_DATA_URI` (line 309), yet `isSafeImageSrc` returns true via the relative branch.

No test covers `<` in an href/src (test/serialize/markdown.test.ts:552-720 covers only schemes, scheme-relative `//`/`\\`, and whitespace/controls), so the gate reads as covered while this hole is open.

samples.summary: HTML entity references let a dangerous scheme through the `HAS_SCHEME` → `isSafeUrl` split, because CommonMark decodes entities inside link destinations
samples.evidence:
`isEmittableUrl` only sends a reference to `isSafeUrl` when the *raw* string matches `HAS_SCHEME` (line 271/298); anything else is accepted as "cannot name a protocol". But CommonMark explicitly recognizes entity and numeric character references inside link destinations (spec example `[foo](/föö)` → `href="/föö"`).

So an attacker-supplied `style.href` of `javascript:alert(1)` starts with `&`, does not match `HAS_SCHEME`, does not match `SCHEME_RELATIVE`, contains no whitespace or controls → emitted verbatim as `[text](javascript:alert(1))`. A CommonMark renderer decodes it to `javascript:alert(1)` and, unless it applies its own scheme sanitizer, produces a live `javascript:` link in a document exported from Wafflebase. The same trick reproduces the scheme-relative case the diff deliberately blocks: `//evil.example/x` decodes to `//evil.example/x`, and it also reaches the image path via `isSafeImageSrc` (line 318). The gate's own premise — "with no scheme they cannot select a dangerous one" (comment at line 291-293) — does not hold once the consumer decodes entities.

samples.summary: Run text is not escaped against block-level Markdown markers, so attacker-supplied text at the start of a paragraph can forge document structure in the export
samples.evidence: `escapeMarkdownText` escapes only `\ * _ [ ] ` ~ <` and folds line separators. It does not escape the block-opening markers `#`, `>`, `-`/`+`, `1.` or `|`. Because a paragraph block's text is written at the very start of an output line (`blockToMarkdown`, line 112-113), a run whose text begins `# Signed by the CEO` or `> quoted approval` — provenance identical to the `href`/`alt` cases the diff hardens (HTML paste, DOCX import, a collaborator's CRDT write) — renders in the exported `.md` as a heading or blockquote the author never wrote. This is content/structure spoofing rather than script execution, and the newline folding added here limits it to block starts, but it is the same injection class the surrounding hardening addresses.

samples.summary: `safeFilename` (now also used for the new .md/.txt downloads) does not strip control characters, bidi overrides, or a leading dot from the document title
samples.evidence: The sanitizer replaces only `\ / : * ? " < > |`. A document title (attacker-influenceable for a shared/collaborated doc) containing e.g. a RTL override or control characters, or beginning with `.`, is carried into the `a.download` value at export-utils.ts:64. Browsers sanitize `download` filenames, so this is defence-in-depth rather than a traversal; the change only widens the extension union, so the weakness is pre-existing and identical for the already-shipped `.pdf`/`.docx` paths (the task doc records it as a known limitation).

verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as described. isEmittableUrl (markdown.ts:295-300) rejects only whitespace/C0-C1 controls (UNEMITTABLE_URL_CHARS, line 263 — does not include `<` or `>`), then branches on HAS_SCHEME (line 271, anchored to `^[A-Za-z]`). A destination starting with `<` matches neither HAS_SCHEME nor SCHEME_RELATIVE (line 280), so it falls through the relative branch and is accepted without ever reaching isSafeUrl's protocol allowlist (packages/core/src/url/index.ts:16-31). escapeMarkdownHref (line 396-398) escapes only `\` and `)`, so the value is emitted verbatim at line 225 and line 341 — while escapeMarkdownText (line 374) escapes `<` in body text, showing the codebase already treats `<` as output-dangerous. CommonMark's angle-bracket link-destination form (with backslash escapes processed inside) makes `[t](<javascript:alert\(1\)>)` resolve to href `javascript:alert(1)`, the exact value the gate exists to block; a non-parsing variant like `<script>...</script>` degrades to literal text where the tags are re-parsed as inline raw HTML. The image path is bypassed the same way: `/^data:/i` at line 330 is false for `<data:text/html;...>` so the placeholder branch is skipped, SAFE_IMAGE_DATA_URI (line 309) fails, and isSafeImageSrc (line 313-318) returns true via isEmittableUrl. No guard exists upstream — the file's own comments (lines 220-223, 250-251, 336-337) state href/src are unvalidated on ingest from HTML/DOCX import, paste and CRDT writes — and serializeMarkdown is reachable from the CLI `docs content --format md` surface and the docs export path. This is a bypassed injection/URL-scheme gate, in-lane and blocking.

finding.summary: HTML entity references let a dangerous scheme through the `HAS_SCHEME` → `isSafeUrl` split, because CommonMark decodes entities inside link destinations
finding.evidence:
`isEmittableUrl` only sends a reference to `isSafeUrl` when the *raw* string matches `HAS_SCHEME` (line 271/298); anything else is accepted as "cannot name a protocol". But CommonMark explicitly recognizes entity and numeric character references inside link destinations (spec example `[foo](/föö)` → `href="/föö"`).

So an attacker-supplied `style.href` of `javascript:alert(1)` starts with `&`, does not match `HAS_SCHEME`, does not match `SCHEME_RELATIVE`, contains no whitespace or controls → emitted verbatim as `[text](javascript:alert(1))`. A CommonMark renderer decodes it to `javascript:alert(1)` and, unless it applies its own scheme sanitizer, produces a live `javascript:` link in a document exported from Wafflebase. The same trick reproduces the scheme-relative case the diff deliberately blocks: `//evil.example/x` decodes to `//evil.example/x`, and it also reaches the image path via `isSafeImageSrc` (line 318). The gate's own premise — "with no scheme they cannot select a dangerous one" (comment at line 291-293) — does not hold once the consumer decodes entities.

verdict.reason: The code is exactly as described. `HAS_SCHEME` (markdown.ts:271) is anchored at `^[A-Za-z]`, so a destination beginning with `&` never reaches `isSafeUrl` (markdown.ts:298); `SCHEME_RELATIVE` (markdown.ts:280) is anchored on literal `/`/`\`; and `UNEMITTABLE_URL_CHARS` (markdown.ts:263) only rejects whitespace and C0/C1 controls. So `javascript:alert(1)` falls through `isEmittableUrl` to `return true` (markdown.ts:299) and is written verbatim into the link destination at markdown.ts:225, since `escapeMarkdownHref` (markdown.ts:396-398) escapes only `\` and `)` and leaves `&` untouched. CommonMark decodes entity/numeric character references inside link destinations, so the consumer resolves it to `javascript:alert(1)`; `//evil.example/x` likewise reconstitutes the scheme-relative origin change that line 280 exists to block, and the image path shares the hole via `isSafeImageSrc` (markdown.ts:313-318). The gate's stated premise (comment at markdown.ts:291-293) is therefore false against an entity-decoding renderer. I searched for an upstream guard and found none: no href entity-decoding/escaping exists in the docs package, and the file's own comments (markdown.ts:219-223, 250-251, 334-337) state these values arrive unvalidated from HTML paste, DOCX import, and collaborator CRDT writes. This is an export-time scheme-allowlist bypass producing a live dangerous-scheme link — injection/unsafe-input-handling, squarely in the security lane, and no named refutation ground applies.

finding.summary: Image `alt` is written into the exported `.md` with only `\` and `]` escaped, so an attacker-controlled alt breaks out of `![...]` and injects raw HTML/Markdown — the same delimiter breakout this change just closed for `href`/`src`
finding.evidence: `escapeMarkdownAlt` (markdown.ts:325-327) escapes only `[\\\]]`. It does NOT escape `<` (which `escapeMarkdownText` at :318 *does* escape for body text) and does not reject newlines, while the new `UNEMITTABLE_URL_CHARS` gate (:263) is applied only to the URL, never to `alt`. `imageInline` (:296, :308) then emits `![${alt}](...)` verbatim. Vector: an attacker supplies `image.alt = "pic\n\n"`. Alt is attacker-influenceable through exactly the ingress paths the diff's own comment cites — `packages/docs/src/view/clipboard.ts:117` copies `alt` straight out of pasted clipboard JSON with no validation, `packages/docs/src/view/editor.ts:3692` takes it from `insertImage({alt})`, and a collaborator can write it over the CRDT. The victim exports Markdown (`packages/frontend/src/app/docs/text-actions.ts` → `serializeMarkdown(doc, {inlineImages:true})`) and the downloaded file contains: ![pic ](https://ok/x.png) The blank line ends the paragraph, so the trailing `` lands as a raw-HTML block in the exported document and fires in any renderer that passes raw HTML through (local previews, static-site generators, `marked`/`markdown-it` with `html: true`). This is precisely the "validator never looks at the bytes we emit" class the change documents at :239-262, left unfixed one line below the fix.

finding.summary: The new `assertUsablePageSetup` guard is bypassed by DOCX import and by any `setDocument` write, so a hostile `.docx` still persists NaN/closed-box page geometry into the CRDT for every collaborator
finding.evidence:
`assertUsablePageSetup` (packages/docs/src/view/editor.ts:960-993) is called only from `writePageSetup` (editor.ts:2062). The comment there states the invariant exists because bad geometry "would be persisted into the CRDT for every collaborator" — but that is not the only write path.

Bypass: `parsePageSetup` (packages/docs/src/import/docx-parser.ts:300-314) takes `w:pgSz/@w:w`, `@w:h` and the four `w:pgMar` values from the uploaded file with `Math.round(twipsToPx(parseInt(v,10)))` and no bounds check at all — `w:w="abc"` yields `NaN`, `w:w="-1000"` yields a negative width, `w:left="9999999"` yields margins far wider than the page. `docx-importer.ts:137,158` returns that as `document.pageSetup`, and the importer's document is stored via `setDocument`, which writes `root.pageSetup` directly (packages/frontend/src/app/docs/yorkie-doc-store.ts:2872-2876 and :2898-2902) — never through `writePageSetup`. Remote CRDT sync (`readPageSetup`, yorkie-doc-store.ts:604) likewise applies whatever a peer wrote with no validation.

So an attacker who can get a victim to import a crafted `.docx` (or who has edit access to a shared doc) stores exactly the state the guard declares unlayoutable, and it is replicated to every collaborator on open — a persistent client-side denial of the document. The added guard covers only the two callers that already respected the rule, which makes the invariant read as enforced when it is not.

verdict.reason: The finding's quoted evidence does not match the repository. (1) `parsePageSetup` is not unchecked: `sectPrLengthPx` (packages/docs/src/import/docx-parser.ts:302-314) rejects non-finite `parseInt` results and zero/negative page dimensions and negative margins, so `w:w="abc"` or `w:w="-11906"` fall back to the Letter default (docx-parser.ts:320-338). (2) The parsed setup is not handed to `setDocument` raw: docx-parser.ts:347 returns `resolvePageSetup(...)`, which re-validates sizes/margins and proportionally shrinks margins that close the content box (packages/docs/src/model/types.ts:759-791, 810-841), guaranteeing a positive box before it ever reaches yorkie-doc-store.ts:2873/2899. (3) The remote-CRDT read is not unvalidated either: `getPageSetup` wraps `readPageSetup` in `resolvePageSetup` (packages/frontend/src/app/docs/yorkie-doc-store.ts:663-665) and every layout consumer resolves first (editor.ts:1372, 2074, 2436, 2973, 3680; store/memory.ts:95; packages/cli/src/docs/paginate.ts:26). The invariant is enforced by clamping on the untrusted read paths and by throwing on the deliberate write (types.ts:793-809), and tests at packages/docs/test/import/docx-parser.test.ts:184-213 exercise precisely the hostile `.docx` inputs cited. No NaN/closed-box geometry is persisted by the described attack.
